summary:
New Mexico sits in the fifteen-state "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, compiled by applying a rubric to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the withdrawal of legal recognition. The ranking's authors describe the laws of this tier as having gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

State law effective 1 July 2003 prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership. The public-accommodations limb is the one a visitor interacts with directly: it covers restaurants, hotels, shops and other places serving the public. The 15-or-more-employees exemption was repealed effective 1 July 2019, and 2023 legislation explicitly extended coverage to local entities, counties, schools, universities and government-run agencies under an emergency clause; Albuquerque amended its Human Rights Ordinance in May 2024 to align.

Since 1 November 2019 transgender people may change legal gender without surgery. Legislation passed 26-13 in the House and 33-14 in the Senate and signed by Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham repealed the 1984 surgery requirement and provides male, female and X neutral designations on birth certificates, driver's licences and state IDs. An applicant submits a Request to Change Gender Designation on a Birth Certificate form with fees, with parental consent for minors, or a Request for Sex Designation Change form to the Motor Vehicles Division for licences and IDs. This replaced a prior requirement for a perjury statement from an institution or physician attesting surgical change plus a certified name-change order.

Since 1 July 2019 businesses and public facilities with single-occupancy restrooms must mark them gender-neutral and available to any person regardless of gender identity or sex, under legislation passed 54-12 in the House and 23-15 in the Senate and signed by the Governor. The state has no law prohibiting transgender girls' sports participation; eligibility is determined by birth certificate, original or amended, and the New Mexico Activities Association has issued no further guidance.

Gender-affirming care is protected rather than restricted. In March 2023 House Bill 7 codified protection for gender-affirming care and sex-reassignment surgery for adults on request without restrictions, including for interstate travellers, and is cited as establishing New Mexico as a refuge for transgender youths. The Movement Advancement Project's Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, data as of 27 September 2026, lists New Mexico as a state holding a shield law or 2023 executive order: the shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where the care is legal in New Mexico but banned in the patient's home state, which is directly relevant to a visitor travelling from a ban state. In 2026 the state health care authority announced use of state funds to maintain Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming care after a federal rule moved to exclude it.

Since 2003 New Mexico's hate-crime law has explicitly covered violence committed on the basis of actual or perceived gender identity. In February 2022 the Legislature passed omnibus crime bill HB68 repealing the common-law gay and trans panic defence, signed 9 March 2022. March 2019 school-bullying legislation protects students on the basis of gender identity and requires districts to adopt prohibition, reporting, investigation, disciplinary, prevention and staff-training policies, effective 1 July 2019.

Same-sex couples have had the same marriage rights as different-sex couples since the 19 December 2013 state Supreme Court ruling requiring equal marriage rights, making New Mexico the 17th state to recognise same-sex marriage; statutory codification passed 62-0 in the House and 39-0 in the Senate in March 2019 and took effect 1 July 2019. A trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status therefore has that relationship recognised here.
tangentialFactors:
The July 2026 ranking's contrast tier shows how far the state sits from the worst-law jurisdictions: those states carry up to five-year prison terms for gender-identity-related offences, as in Idaho, or an arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use, as in Florida. New Mexico's tier is one of fifteen, alongside California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington.

The national shield picture around New Mexico is uneven. MAP's map records 16 states plus Washington, D.C., covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, as holding shields, while 32 states and 5 territories, covering 56%, hold none; youth-care bans are tracked nationally with some permanently blocked in court.

Statewide polling shows sustained but dated public support for the statutory framework: 73% supported anti-discrimination legislation protecting LGBTQ people in 2018, and 64% supported a law covering sexual orientation and gender identity in 2017. Santa Fe is cited as a gay capital and Albuquerque, including its metropolitan area, as a gay-friendly city.

Indigenous gender traditions in the region predate the current legal regime. The Navajo recognised four gender roles including nadleehi, a male-bodied person with a feminine nature, who was typically chosen for communal and spiritual roles, wore female clothing and did female work, and could have sexual relations with men, which the tribe accepted; comparable recognised roles existed among the Zuni (lhamana and katsotse) and among Mescalero Apache, Tiwa, Tewa and other pueblos. Colonisation eroded this acceptance: nadleehi became a subject of ridicule, and Christian converts among the Hopi were prohibited from attending the traditional snake dance because male cross-dressing could be observed. Will Roscoe is documented as writing that the "tolerance or even respect of transgender people" was used by Spanish explorers to argue for colonisation in the name of Christianity. Today LGBTQ Navajo may find it difficult to be accepted by family.
localsOnly:
Residents have a statutory non-discrimination entitlement dating from 1 July 2003 across employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership, with the 15-or-more-employees exemption removed effective 1 July 2019 and 2023 legislation extending coverage expressly to local entities, counties, schools, universities and government-run agencies under an emergency clause. Albuquerque aligned its Human Rights Ordinance in May 2024.

Legal gender change for residents requires no surgery and no medical evidence: a Request to Change Gender Designation on a Birth Certificate form with the applicable fees, with parental consent for minors, or a Request for Sex Designation Change form to the Motor Vehicles Division for a licence or state ID. Male, female and X designations are available on birth certificates, driver's licences and state IDs. House Bill 31, passed in 2023, repealed the requirement to publish a legal name change in a newspaper, which had risked the privacy, safety and lives of transgender individuals.

Students are covered by March 2019 bullying legislation requiring districts to adopt prohibition, reporting, investigation, disciplinary, prevention and staff-training policies on the basis of gender identity, effective 1 July 2019. Sexual orientation change efforts on minors are prohibited under SB121, passed 32-6 in the Senate and 44-23 in the House and signed 7 April 2017 by Governor Susana Martinez, effective 6 July 2017.

Residents retain access to gender-affirming care under House Bill 7 (March 2023), and in 2026 the state health care authority announced that state funds would maintain Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming care after a federal rule moved to exclude it. Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity is also addressed by state law, and enforcement of the state's non-discrimination regime was upheld unanimously in Elane Photography v. Willock in 2013.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific violence incidents, homicide counts or enforcement outcomes for New Mexico's hate-crime or non-discrimination provisions appear in this inventory; the absence of documented cases is not evidence of their non-occurrence, and no period of observation is given.

How New Mexico's X designation on state IDs and birth certificates interacts with federal document rules for a resident crossing the border is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

The inventory reports that 70% of LGBT Navajo youth have attempted suicide without giving a survey date, a sample, a methodology or a trans-specific breakdown; the figure is not carried into the assessment above for that reason.

Whether House Bill 7's "on request" standard applies to non-resident minors travelling for care, and what documentation a visiting minor would need, is not specified in the sources. The New Mexico Activities Association's silence on further eligibility guidance is recorded as an absence of guidance rather than a stated rule.

Public-opinion figures cited are from 2017 and 2018 and measure support for LGBTQ anti-discrimination legislation generally, not current trans-specific prevalence or attitudes.
